entries.text: Some of the best technical insights come from sharing what you've built and what you've learned along the way. That's one of the core ideas behind Unprompted, the blog we launched on Medium earlier this year to give Grafana Labs engineers and our broader OSS community a space to showcase their work. From behind-the-scenes engineering stories and technical deep dives to creative use cases for Grafana (a fishing dashboard, anyone?), it's a place to share ideas and learn from one another. To give you a sense of what you'll find, we've rounded up a few recent posts covering everything from Grafana's architecture to monitoring your favorite reality TV show. Behind the scenes at Grafana Labs These posts explore some of the technical challenges our teams have tackled at Grafana Labs, including the decisions, tradeoffs, and lessons that shaped their work. Our journey to improve Grafana Assistant dashboarding mode Making an AI agent faster, more reliable, and less expensive takes a lot more than fine-tuning your prompts. Senior Software Engineer Dominik Broj shares how the team used production telemetry, offline evaluations, and Agent Observability to improve dashboarding mode in Grafana Assistant, reducing error rates by 73%, latency p95 by 50%, and cost by 18%. How and why we're bringing data sources out of the Grafana monolith Grafana data sources have historically been closely tied to the Grafana monolith. entries.summary: Grafana Labs does not have a headquarters office. Since its founding in 2014, it has been fully remote-first.
entries.text: Grafana Labs does not have a headquarters office. Since its founding in 2014, it has been fully remote-first. It began with three co-founders living on different continents, and today our team spans more than 50 countries. From day one, the organization was designed with the assumption that everyone works remotely. Real-time meetings are kept to a minimum, information is shared through documentation, and we have cultivated a culture that trusts people to “work autonomously.” At its core lies the transparency and autonomy of open source. And now, we are building the world’s first Executive Briefing Center (EBC) in Ginza, Tokyo. A remote-first company creating a physical space—what does that mean? This article is the first in a three-part series following the EBC launch project. From the background of the concept to site selection, design philosophy, and even the demolition process, we will walk you through the journey. Not an “office,” but an “EBC” We do not call this place an “office.” It is an Executive Briefing Center, or EBC for short. As a remote-first company, there is no need to commute to a fixed location every day. However, there has never been a place anywhere in the world where people can directly experience the Grafana product, or share the same physical space with customers and the community to engage with technology. The EBC is designed to serve three roles. A place to experience the product A space where customers can directly interact with Grafana solutions, ex
entries.title: Grafana Labs’ First Executive Briefing Center Coming to Ginza

entries.summary: A teammate asks why you think a deployment caused checkout failures.
entries.text: A teammate asks why you think a deployment caused checkout failures. You have an error-rate chart in your dashboard, a query that narrows the failures to one payment provider, and an explanation you've been exploring with Grafana Assistant. To bring your teammate up to speed, you start collecting screenshots and query links, then write out how they connect. That explanation is part of the analysis. Your teammate needs to see what supports the conclusion and where you're still making an assumption. As findings come from both your own exploration in Grafana and from AI-assisted work, having one place to examine them together becomes key. Grafana Notebooks help you do just that, bringing charts, queries, and findings from Assistant together in one working document, so teammates can follow your reasoning and assess next steps. In this post, we’ll use the checkout example above to show how this works in practice, then look at how Notebooks can support rollout decisions and post-incident reviews. How Notebooks work: develop your analysis in a working document Through conversations with users, we've heard a recurring need for a lightweight place to work through a question and share the results. Notebooks give that work room to develop inside Grafana, from an initial observation to a recommendation someone can assess. You can start with a panel you've already found. Select Add to notebook from its dashboard menu, or from the Add menu in Explore, and choose a new or existing notebook.
entries.title: Bring charts, queries, and context into one shareable document: Introducing Grafana Notebooks

entries.summary: A support ticket comes in with one clue: a transaction ID. The answer is somewhere in your logs, but you don't know which service logged it, which pod handled it, or which day it happened.
entries.text: A support ticket comes in with one clue: a transaction ID. The answer is somewhere in your logs, but you don't know which service logged it, which pod handled it, or which day it happened. So you write the query you always write, {service="payments"} |= "txn-123456", widen the time range to the last two weeks, and wait. Then the query times out. Loki was originally built around a simple idea: index labels, not log content, and store compressed logs cheaply in object storage. That design keeps storage costs low and operations light, and it's why teams keep choosing Loki and Grafana Cloud Logs, the fully managed log aggregation system powered by Loki, as their log volumes grow. For most queries, this model works very well. But when you search for a highly unique value, like a request ID, job ID, user ID, or device ID, labels can only narrow the search so far. Loki still has to read a lot of raw log data to find a handful of matching lines. At terabyte and petabyte scale, that process can be slow and costly. To fix that, we built full-text search for Grafana Cloud Logs, a capability based on the Logline technology Grafana Labs acquired in April 2026. Full-text search, now generally available in Grafana Cloud Logs, adds a purpose-built secondary index to Loki, so you can find specific log lines across weeks of logs in seconds without a full scan. You go straight to the one transaction ID, user ID, or error that matters and cut time to resolution. “When I ran our first query on ne
entries.title: Find the log line that matters faster with full-text search in Grafana Cloud Logs

entries.summary: When an application slows down or memory usage keeps climbing, knowing which code is responsible can help you find a fix faster.
entries.text: When an application slows down or memory usage keeps climbing, knowing which code is responsible can help you find a fix faster. Continuous profiling gives you that visibility, so you can see where your application spends resources such as CPU time and memory. We’ve made updates to Pyroscope, our open source continuous profiling database, that make it easier to profile your applications, find performance bottlenecks, and optimize your code, whether you're doing the work yourself or with an AI agent. Highlights include: Profile more of your workloads: Memory profiling for Python and Rust, and .NET support on Windows, helps you find performance bottlenecks across more of your services. Let AI agents work with your profiling data: Pyroscope commands in gcx, the Grafana CLI, let an agent query your profiles directly. See more of your profiling data in Grafana: Exemplars and a new Call Tree view help you explore your profiles visually, whether you're investigating on your own or looking at what an agent found. Many of these capabilities build directly on Pyroscope 2.0, the ground-up rearchitecture of Pyroscope that makes continuous profiling more cost-effective at scale (in our production environment, it reduced the symbol storage footprint by up to 95%). For example, exemplars require the v2 storage layer that Pyroscope 2.0 is built on. Read on to learn more about some of the latest updates. And for a full list of recent changes, see the release notes for Pyroscope and Profiles D
entries.title: What's new in Pyroscope: profile more of your workflows, troubleshoot with AI agents, and more

entries.summary: Whether you’re investigating an incident or just exploring your data, a clear, consistent UI helps you move between workflows and find what matters faster.
entries.text: Whether you’re investigating an incident or just exploring your data, a clear, consistent UI helps you move between workflows and find what matters faster. As Grafana has grown to support more use cases, we’ve seen opportunities to improve on that experience. That’s why, as part of the Grafana 13.3 release, we introduced the first phase of our biggest visual refresh since Grafana 7. We’re approaching this work in phases, with the refreshed UI currently in public preview in both Grafana Cloud and self-managed versions of Grafana, and your feedback will play a major role in shaping what comes next. In this post, we’ll give you a closer look at why we decided to make this change now, why we think visual aesthetics matter in a UI, and the impact this will have on the Grafana user experience. You can also check out some of the visual updates in the video below. Starting with why “Purposes are deduced from behavior, not from rhetoric or stated goals.” – Donella Meadows At Grafana Labs, our culture empowers individuals and teams to identify user needs, build solutions quickly, ship iteratively, and work in the open. This has allowed us to cover a large range of use cases with Grafana. But moving fast can come with challenges, including design debt, which leads to inconsistent and sometimes conflicting visual cues, workflows, and GUIs. We were aware of these challenges, but our focus remained steadfast on providing new functionality and supporting as many use cases as possible. Meanw
entries.title: An early look at the Grafana UI refresh: Building a clearer, more consistent user experience

entries.summary: Alert rules are great for the failures you can predict, but they fall short on the ones you can't.
entries.text: Alert rules are great for the failures you can predict, but they fall short on the ones you can't. With the advent of modern AI, you might think the solution is to swarm your stack with agents that monitor every last detail, but that can quickly lead to astronomical bills. And those are the gaps Watchers fill: catching what alerts miss while keeping costs in control. Generally Available as of ObservabilityCON 2026, Watchers are always-on agents in Grafana Assistant. You describe what to monitor (in natural language) and pick your data sources, and the watcher learns what "normal" looks like and tells you when you drift from that state. Ultimately, this helps you surface problems without needing an alert, giving you wider coverage and more confidence in your system. But how do we keep Watchers cost-effective for our customers, especially in comparison to building your own agent that runn around the clock? For example, let's say you deploy your own version of a watcher that checks in every 10 minutes, which means it runs 4,320 times a month. If each run were an agentic investigation, which cost us between $0.56 and $1.26 in a recent experiment, that one watcher you built would cost thousands of dollars a month. Yet the Watchers running on our own Grafana Cloud stack cost a median of less than $5 a month. In this post, I'll show you the engineering behind that number, which mostly comes down to one question: where do you actually need an LLM's intelligence, and how much of it? T
entries.title: Run cost-effective, always-on agents to monitor your environment: the engineering behind Watchers

entries.summary: AI agents are becoming part of everyday engineering workflows, helping teams write code, troubleshoot issues, and automate tasks.
entries.text: AI agents are becoming part of everyday engineering workflows, helping teams write code, troubleshoot issues, and automate tasks. But to be truly useful in production, these agents need access to more than code. They also need observability data and context to understand what's happening across your systems, investigate problems, and help you take action. At Grafana Labs, we believe that context should be available wherever you work. That’s one of the core ideas behind Grafana Cloud as the open agentic observability platform: the flexibility to work with your observability data through the AI agents you prefer—whether it’s Grafana Assistant, a coding agent in your IDE, or a tool you’ve built yourself—so you can investigate and troubleshoot issues without switching tools. In this post, we'll explore how to bring Grafana Cloud into your agentic workflows using tools like the Grafana Cloud MCP server and gcx, with practical examples along the way. You can also check out our ObservabilityCON 2026 talk in the video below to learn more. Three ways to use Grafana Cloud with AI agents There are multiple ways to bring Grafana Cloud observability data and context into your AI workflows, depending on where and how you prefer to work: Work directly in Grafana Cloud: Use Grafana Assistant, the AI-powered assistant built into Grafana Cloud, to investigate issues and interact with your observability data. Connect your preferred AI agent: Use the Grafana Cloud MCP server to bring Grafana Clo
entries.title: Any agent anywhere: How to use Grafana Cloud with Claude, Cursor, and any other AI agent

entries.summary: Template variables are one of the most used features in Grafana, providing users with a dropdown to turn one dashboard into hundreds: pick a different cluster, region, or service, and every panel updates.
entries.text: Template variables are one of the most used features in Grafana, providing users with a dropdown to turn one dashboard into hundreds: pick a different cluster, region, or service, and every panel updates. For most of Grafana's history, variables had a single home at the top of the dashboard. Each dashboard had one flat list of variables, and that list was shared by every panel on it. But as dashboards grew in size and number, those controls became harder to organize and maintain. The top of a dashboard could get crowded with dropdowns that only applied to certain panels, while shared controls were copied across dashboards and had to be updated individually. To address these challenges, we’ve rolled out two new features in Grafana: Section-level variables for rows and tabs (generally available): these variables let you place controls near the panels they affect, reducing clutter at the top of the dashboard. Cross-dashboard variables (public preview): these are variables you can define once and reuse across dashboards, keeping configurations consistent and easier to maintain. In this post, we’ll take a closer look at each variable type, its use cases, and how to get started. Section-level variables: define and manage variables by row or tab Section-level variables let you define variables and filters for a specific row or tab, so they apply only to the panels inside that section. entries.title: What’s new with Grafana variables: less clutter, easier reuse across dashboards, and more
